614.t: Gregory Herbert, a virtuoso who stayed himself
614.s: Herman praises Gregory Herbert as a phenomenal saxophonist and flutist who carried tradition while remaining himself.
614.ch: Instruments, tenors and the current band
614.q: Well, whatever, I was proud of most of those guys, believe me, because they were expressing their own thoughts, to a great degree.

614.t: Frank Tiberi: ten years in the band and his complex tenor playing
614.s: Tiberi has been with Herman ten years and brought in Gregory Herbert; Herman admits he often cannot follow Tiberi's complex tenor playing.
614.q: Yeah. And I'll confess with no qualms at all that for the first couple of years I couldn't understand Frank's tenor playing at all. And after ten years, I'm not sure I do all the time.

614.t: Nistico's European work and place in the Herds
614.s: Wong mentions a German big band album with Nistico; both agree he set a model as a swinger, while Herbert's value lay in other facets.
614.ch: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
614.q: Yeah, it was his other facets that were really more important, I thought, his ballad facets and doubles and so on.

614.t: Nick Brignola, a stomping baritone saxophonist
614.s: Herman calls Brignola, from upstate New York, one of the real giants of baritone in 15 years, with a spirit established players lack.
614.ch: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
614.q: There's a baritone saxophonists that I think is one of the real giants in the last 15 years or more, and who's a contemporary of, once again, that area of upstate New York, northern New York.

614.t: Baritone players: Serge Chaloff, Hipner, Johnson, Smulyan
614.s: Frank Hipner was a strange but outstanding player now in Reno; Bruce Johnson is outstanding, and Gary Smulyan from Long Island is a brilliant current player.
614.ch: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
614.q: spirit in every direction, and that kind of player. He was heavily influenced by the early bop music, and he played baritone somewhat like Charlie Parker played alto. It was that --

70.t: Pete Brown and Earle Warren, alto saxophonists
70.s: Pete Brown was a jolly swinging alto of the 52nd Street days; Jackson also praises his Springfield friend Earle Warren as an underrated first alto with Basie.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: And he used to play in the Village quite a bit, too, just like the trumpet player I was speaking about, Frankie Newton, played in the Village for years. But Pete Brown was a fixture.

70.s: Tab Smith, whom he knew with Lucky Millinder, had a Hodges-like feel and later played with Basie alongside Earle Warren.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh, gee. He was another influence on a lot of alto players. I knew Tab when he first came with Lucky Millinder in the thirties. He was a great influence. He made a lot of good records.

474.s: David Jones, Son Johnson, Handy, Bostic, Guy Kelly and Herman Franklin.
474.ch: Hometown ties, community and favorite players
474.q: Yeah, Professor David Jones. Oh. Then you had Hanny. Hanny was of his time. Mm-hmm. Then you had another fellow by the name of Edgar Solskjaer. Mm-hmm. Then you had Son Johnson. Mm-hmm. But Son Johnson was about to, in the later years to come, he was about to, was the greatest saxophone club we had…

765.t: Schiro's saxophone style and other sax players
765.s: He didn't copy anyone; talk of Eddie Miller, Lester Lushon and three-tenor arrangements.
765.q: I never heard Lester Nelson. They say he was good. Yeah, he was good. He and Australia used to team up things. Oh yeah. And what was another saxophone? I think they had three, sometimes they had three tenner sometimes. Oh, some big.

828.t: Alto and baritone players, Excelsior band and Manuel Gabriel
828.s: Lanoix recalls baritone and alto players, the Excelsior band led by Charles Moret, and Manuel Gabriel on clarinet.
828.ch: Bass horn, tubas and Kid Rena
828.q: One was, I don't remember the alto, I don't remember one alto player, he just died. Paul Barberin's father and Cisador Barberin. He was one and Adolf Alexander, I don't know if you remember. I know his son, no. His daddy, I mean the dad. Well he played a good baritone too, the son. And what he had…

190.t: Son Johnson, the alto and piano player with endless breath
190.s: They remember Son Johnson, an alto and piano player who sat while others stood and who could play long phrases without a breath.
190.q: See, you blow from his diaphragm, you see. Well, before anybody around, they knew anything about all that, you know, he was a that. That kid could play from now until you walk to the corner and back and don't take no breath.

191.t: Rudy Wiedoeft and Boyd Senter as saxophone and clarinet influences
191.s: Kelly praises Wiedoeft's popularizing of saxophone and says he copied Boyd Senter's records.
191.q: Rudy Weidoff was extremely popular. Uh, he was a concert artist and, uh, a very popular Victor recording artist and, uh, is not given credit enough for the influence he had in popularizing the saxophone. Certainly he not only wrote for it, but he played it well and his records were sold by the…

776.s: Brief exchange about Norman Mason, who played saxophone and at one time cornet.
776.q: Yeah, right? Yeah. Oh, wow. I haven't seen him here. He looks very strong and healthy. He's looking as a pleasant color. Uh-huh, he's alright. He's a good color on here.

841.t: Admired alto players: John Handy, Sonny Johnson and Oliver Alcorn
841.s: Harris names the best early saxophonists in New Orleans and gives his opinions of them.
841.q: just wanted to do is John Handy was one now that's the boy I used to admire when he was blowing he was blowing everybody John Handy said old pioneer yeah and uh Tats what his name Tate's or Tats? Adolf Alexander Tats Tats son Johnson and that's a master oh that was a master yeah boy I'm sure I'll…

405.t: Mixed feelings about Preservation Hall and John Handy
405.s: With the remarks restricted, Bull calls the Hall's set-up strange, praises Elton Purnell and John Handy, and objects that Handy is not used because he plays saxophone.
405.q: Well to me the whole set up in, in, in preservation hall is, uh, uh, it's a little bit, uh, a little bit confusing, a bit strange, a bit sick. This business of, uh, of having a bloke, uh, front a band which he doesn't pick and things like this, uh, just isn't, doesn't seem right to me. Uh, anyway I…

476.t: Edgar Sosia's modern sax and the trumpeter Kuyper
476.s: Edgar Sosia played what became rock and roll licks; Kuyper was another trumpeter with the band, from the Entertainers, who played in a Louis Armstrong style.
476.q: Kuyper, who was he great? Yes sir. The run of the sun went out of the joint. He was playing at the tannifor. He was playing at the entertainers for a long time. Louis Primm and I used to go there every night and listen at him. He was in the entertainers.

639.t: Saxophones, Eddie Miller, and Snoozer Quinn among the greatest
639.s: He defends the saxophone through Eddie Miller on tenor, then ranks Bix, Louis Armstrong and Snoozer Quinn as the greatest he heard.
639.q: audience don't like a saxophone and uh uh i'm not going to say that uh i'm going to put it this way it doesn't make any difference what instrument a man plays if he plays it uh uh wonderfully then i'm i'm going to like it like i told you before i don't care if he's playing on the top of a crawfish…

311.t: Jerry Dodgion and playing with great names
311.s: He recalls saxophonist Jerry Dodgion in his band and says good players make you play better.
311.q: Oh yeah. Jerry Dodgion is a nice guy. See I had them all in this band. I played with some great guys.

467.t: Josh Redman on the 1990s 'Flyin' Home' recording
467.s: Hampton praises Joshua Redman's tenor solo on a recent version of the tune; they discuss his father Dewey Redman and his Harvard background.
467.q: The guy that’s playing the tenor part on there, it goes on the jacket there that he plays the tenor part, naturally will become very famous. It’s a guy by the name of Josh Redman. And he’s a guy that’s making a whole lot of noise now with his saxophone playing. And he’s playing on this. I’d like to…

490.t: Dexter Gordon and the bebop era
490.s: Harris says Dexter Gordon was close to but not quite bebop, and places the great saxophonists.
490.q: Well, his is slightly different, it’s not Bird, but it’s slightly different. He was around a long time, you know, Dexter was around at the beginning of Bird.

85.t: Other saxophonists: Wayne King, Rudy Wiedoft, Leonard Fields
85.s: Carter discusses saxophonists whose sound or technique impressed him.
85.q: Well, you know, I can’t remember that there was anybody that influenced me. I know that I used to like the sound of Wayne King, the instrument, you know, the sound he got out of the instrument, and he was the melody player. Gee, I don’t know.

505.t: Wayne Shorter's articulation enters his tenor playing
505.s: After returning to tenor, Liebman heard Shorter's speech-like articulation appearing in his own playing.
505.q: He had never been an influence. I mean, he was an influence, but his way of playing had never influenced me in my formative – in the ’60s and ’70s. Compositionally, of course, and Miles, what we discussed as far as the band and all that, but I never sat and really copped Wayne. In some ways, I…

228.t: Other altoists: Ornette, Bartz, Desmond, Coleman, Lake, Jenkins, Sharpe
228.s: McLean gives quick opinions on Ornette Coleman, Gary Bartz, Desmond, Kenny Garrett, Steve Coleman, Oliver Lake, John Jenkins and Cee Sharpe.
228.ch: Alto sound, teachers and fellow altoists
228.q: Yeah, I like Ornette. He’s a good alto player. I like him because he stood his ground and took the slings and arrows when it was a real hard time for him to do what he

63.t: Sidemen Rudy Tanza, Ralph Roselund and Herbie Steward; Vache and Woody Shaw
63.s: Talbot and Shaw discuss his wartime saxophonists, especially Herbie Steward's musicality, and musical modern players today.
63.ch: Jazz, its audience and the 1953 records
63.q: I have no idea. Once the musicians came back out of this, they probably couldn’t get work. Went into something else. But [tenor saxophonist Ralph] Roselund I remember he had very good control of his horn. He could do things . . . Herbie did most of the solos. But a couple of the things I let…

1.t: David Jones changes New York saxophone style
1.s: Danny says Lee Collins told him that David Jones with the Missourians taught New York saxophonists to play legato, and he was respected like Benny Carter.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: David Jones, yeah. A fantastic musician. He's the man that when he went to New York with the Missourians... He went to St. Louis, he joined R.Q. Dixon and them in Missouri, and he went to New York. And he was a terrific tenor saxophone player. He played legato. See, Hawk and them people in New York…

68.s: Tate says Illinois Jacquet started the single-note honking style, and jokes that Texas stages were big.
68.q: that. Now, Prez could do more with one note than anybody I've seen, you know, like (HUMMING) and all that kind of stuff. Well, now, that's Prez.

146.t: Redman and Carter as altoists with a pocket mouthpiece
146.s: Smith calls Redman a technical altoist with beautiful tone who rented saxophones, and Carter the better player.
146.ch: Looking back and the New York years
146.q: Great. He was great. But he was a key man, what you call a key man. He played with a beautiful tone and beautiful technique. He ain't carin' about all that hot stuff. What he played was beautiful, all that technical stuff. And

0.t: Frankie Trumbauer, C-melody and keeping one's own style
0.s: He remarks on the C-melody saxophone, Trumbauer's advice to stay on tenor and Hawkins praising his independence from others' influence.
0.ch: Coleman Hawkins, Bernie Young and doubling on tenor
0.q: I was good friends. He used to tell me, said, you were on alto, said, why did you go back to tenor? I said, I like the tenor better. He said, stay on it. And Hawk always told me, he says, look, says, you got -- one thing about it I like about you. You don't let nobody influence you. He said, you…

90.s: Johnny Bothwell, Hal McIntyre, Dave Matthews and Sam Donohue as players who broke from the heavy-vibrato mold.
90.q: And I still kept my ears tuned to the radio quite a bit, and listened to the records on the jukebox, and I had my choice of people I liked, and I went ahead with people that, you know, I was impressed by.

381.t: Bootin' tenor: Sam Taylor, Red Prysock and King Curtis's chicken sound
381.s: Francis describes the swinging 'bootin' tenor' sound and how King Curtis copied Sam Taylor before adding his chicken sound on Charlie Brown.
381.ch: Tenor players, tours and band boys
381.q: Yeah, but the funny thing about that -- these guys weren't making funny sounds; guys like Sam Taylor, who were playing what they called bootin' tenor, you know bootin' tenor; it wasn't all these wild, funny sounds.

232.s: Love asks about the southwest tenor sound; Fields says all had a big tone and swing, naming Bert Jones, Hal Singer, Jacquet and Arnett Cobb.
232.ch: Touring in the bus years and Jim Crow in the South
232.q: One thing about it is, it's a funny thing, but it seemed like that all of them had a big tone; they didn't have this little tone and you talk about soul, it seemed like they were like Duke. You might read it soul but you might be calling it swing, and Duke said, don't mean a thing if it ain't got…

73.t: Preston Love and C. Q. Price
73.s: Greene says Preston idolized Earl Warren and that C. Q. Price was a third alto from Buffalo.
73.q: But, he sounded good. He sounded good with the band. I didn't know too much about his background, you know, more or less, but --

124.t: Lunceford's alto and sax section: Willie Smith and Hilton Jefferson
124.s: McRae rates Willie Smith, Chauncey Haughton and Hilton Jefferson against Johnny Hodges and Benny Carter.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: Willie Smith was my sweetheart, man. He was some -- Now you talk about an alto player, that is one of the greatest alto players. They named him and Johnny Hodges two of the greatest that ever lived. Willie Smith and Johnny Hodges and Chauncey Horton. Chick's tenor player --
